title: The towers
hookLine: Marpa has him build towers and tear them down, again and again

cards: Milarepa finally finds Marpa, the farmer-translator, plowing a field. He bows and asks for the teaching, offering himself, body, speech and mind.
And Marpa, the teacher he has wept just to hear named, says something like this: fine, but you can't have food and teaching both. Choose. Milarepa has nothing to offer but his own two hands.
So Marpa points to a ridge and gives him a job. Build me a tower.

teach.b: Milarepa hauls stones on his back and builds the tower, alone. When it's partly done, Marpa comes to look and says he wasn't thinking clearly when he asked for it.
Tear it down, and put every stone back where you found it. A new spot, a new shape, a new tower.
Again Marpa changes his mind. Again it comes down. The story repeats it, and each time Milarepa's back grows more raw from the stones, and still no teaching comes.
Marpa's wife, Dagmema, sees it all and pleads for him.
She even helps him with a trick to win some teaching from another student, which Marpa later uncovers. Milarepa despairs and nearly gives up. Then, in the story, Marpa explains.
The towers were never about towers. Milarepa had done terrible harm, and the endless labor, borne without anger, was a way to purify it. Marpa's harshness, he says, was itself the teaching.
At last he accepts Milarepa as his student. The story is extreme, and it's about one student with one past; it's no rulebook for how a teacher may treat anyone.

What it offers the rest of us is the rhythm: build, take it down, build again, without bitterness. And the week behind us: Shantideva's exchange of self and other. Atisha's lamp, and his cook for patience.
Naropa serving Tilopa. Marpa walking to India and back. Milarepa turning from harm.
And today, he picks up the first stone.

how: Tibetan teachers tell the story of Milarepa's towers as a teaching on purifying past harm and on perseverance, and in the Kagyu tradition a tower in southern Tibet is honored as the one tradition says Milarepa finally completed for Marpa's son.

games.q: you're Milarepa. you've built a tower for Marpa, your back is raw, and he tells you to tear it down and put the stones back. what do you do?
o: tear it down and build again.
argue until he admits he's wrong.
games.why: Milarepa tore it down and built again, more than once, before Marpa finally accepted him.

practice: Rest with the breath, and when your attention wanders off to a plan, a worry or a sound, don't scold it: set the stone down where you found it, and come back, like starting a new tower.
Again, and again; each return is the practice, not a failure of it.

wordCard.voice: The towers. The ones Marpa had Milarepa build and tear down, again and again, as a way to purify his past. Today's word.

carryVoice: Your line: build it again. The labor, borne without anger, was the teaching. And that's the week.

sources.ref: The Life of Milarepa (Tsangnyön Heruka), Milarepa's ordeals with Marpa
